title: Mapping Which Harm Categories Are Most Underprotected in Current Safety Benchmarks
original_idea: Run a standardized set of 10 prompts per harm category across 10 categories on 3 models. Measure ASR per category and compare to the category's frequency in training data proxies (e.g., SafeRLHF dataset category distribution). Identify categories with highest ASR.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Directly actionable: revealing systematic bias in safety training effort across harm categories would guide alignment teams to address underprotected areas.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Straightforward experimental design: write prompts per category, run inference, measure ASR. Comparing against training data proxies adds slight complexity. Medium compute handles 3 models easily.

narrow_scope.reasoning: 10 categories x 10 prompts x 3 models is manageable but crafting 100 quality prompts spanning 10 harm categories and sourcing training data distribution proxies broadens scope.

novelty.reasoning: The paper 'How Should AI Safety Benchmarks Benchmark Safety?' (arxiv 2601.23112) directly examines structural gaps in safety benchmarks, noting that tool-use vulnerabilities and multi-step reasoning failures remain largely unexplored while well-documented ML phenomena rarely transfer into safety evaluation. The FLI AI Safety Index also maps coverage gaps across harm categories. However, the specific methodology of measuring ASR per category and comparing against training data distribution proxies (e.g., SafeRLHF category distribution) is not directly replicated in existing work. The idea adds a quantitative training-data-proxy angle that is partially novel.
